title: Kitab Suwar al-Kawakib al-Thabita (Book of the Fixed Stars)
author: Abd al-Rahman al-Sufi
notes: Digitized on Digital Bodleian; independently corroborated on Wikipedia, Wikimedia Commons, historyofinformation.com, and Ian Ridpath's Star Tales. Note: some scholarship raises doubts about the 1009/1010 colophon date, suggesting the actual manuscript may postdate it by ~150 years -- does not affect al-Sufi's own 964 CE authorship date, only the specific surviving copy's age.

author: Anonymous Syrian or Mesopotamian metalsmith

title: Astrolabe Rete Inscriptions (T.1959.62)
author: Anonymous Moorish metalsmith (13th-c. replacement rete)
notes: Confirmed via National Museums Scotland's own page: the base astrolabe was made by Muhammad ibn al-Saffar, Cordoba, 1026-1027 AD; the rete carrying the star pointers is independently confirmed to be a later, probably 13th-century, replacement -- consistent with this registry's separate dating of the rete inscriptions (1200-1300) from the instrument's own manufacture date.

title: Typen von Sternverzeichnissen: Type I (Maslama al-Majriti / al-Khwarizmi Tradition)
author: Maslama al-Majriti (adapt.) / P. Kunitzsch (ed.)
url_or_citation: Kunitzsch (1966), Typen von Sternverzeichnissen in astronomischen Handschriften des zehnten bis vierzehnten Jahrhunderts, Harrassowitz
notes: Kunitzsch's 1966 monograph (177 star lists in 17 types) is independently confirmed real and is the standard reference this lexicon leans on throughout. This specific Type I entry is not actually cited by any of the 307 attestation rows in the v3 lexicon (matches v3_audit finding F007, MINOR) and is dropped from active use in the remediated lexicon; retained here only as a verified-but-unused registry entry.

title: Typen von Sternverzeichnissen: Type II (Pseudo-Messahalla Star List)
author: Pseudo-Messahalla / P. Kunitzsch (ed.)
notes: BL Arundel 268 independently confirmed to contain a "Compositio"-type astrolabe treatise attributed to Pseudo-Masha'allah, consistent with the registry's claim.

title: Typen von Sternverzeichnissen: Type III (Johannes Hispalensis / John of Seville)
author: Johannes Hispalensis (John of Seville) / P. Kunitzsch (ed.)
notes: BnF lat. 16208 independently confirmed real (late-12th/early-13th-c. astronomical/astrological miscellany, ~136 folios, includes "Hermanus, de astrolabio" among other texts per Biblissima/PAL catalogue records); its association with John of Seville specifically, as opposed to other astrolabe-treatise authors bound in the same miscellany, was not independently pinned down in this remediation. John of Seville himself and his astrolabe-treatise attribution controversy (real name later shown by Kunitzsch to be partly Ibn al-Saffar's work) are independently well documented. Downgraded from the v3 registry's unqualified confidence to PARTIALLY_CONFIRMED.

title: Vienna Astrolabe Star Table (MS Vienna ONB 5415)
author: Vienna Astronomical-Mathematical School (attribution to Johannes von Gmunden personally not independently confirmed)
url_or_citation: Kunitzsch, Typen von Sternverzeichnissen, Type XV (Cod. 5415, fol. 129v per Kunitzsch 1970, cited in Kunitzsch 1986)
notes: ÖNB Cod. 5415 independently confirmed real via Handschriftencensus (Kunitzsch's Type XV is specifically placed at fol. 129v of this codex) and via "Die Wiener Sternkarten von 1435" (a real scholarly study of this exact manuscript's celestial cartography, matching the 1435 date). CAVEATS: (1) personal authorship by Johannes von Gmunden is not independently confirmed -- secondary sources describe the codex as a product of "the early Viennese Astronomical-Mathematical School" without naming him as its author; (2) one independent source places a "fixed star table" folio at 223r and a "celestial map" folio at 168r within the same codex, which does not cleanly match this lexicon's claimed fols. 168r-172v range for the star TABLE specifically -- this remediation could not resolve whether the lexicon's folio range refers to the table or the map. Despite these caveats, the source itself, its date, and its Type XV classification are real; the caveats explain, but do not by themselves prove, why this source turned out to have the highest confirmed defect rate (4 of 12 rows) in the whole lexicon -- see LEXICON_REMEDIATION_REPORT.md.
